title: Seven People Are Running to Lead the United Nations
summary:
The United Nations is about to pick a new leader — and for the first time, it could be a woman. Seven candidates are running to become the next secretary-general, and four of them are women.

The secretary-general is the top official of the United Nations. The job is described as part diplomat, part advocate, part civil servant, and part CEO. The current leader, António Guterres, finishes at the end of the year. The new person starts on January 1, 2027.

The candidates come from different countries. They include Ivonne A-Baki from Ecuador, María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés, also from Ecuador, Rafael Mariano Grossi from Argentina, Rebeca Grynspan Mayufis from Costa Rica, Olara Otunnu from Uganda, Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett from Guyana, and Macky Sall from Senegal.

How does the selection work? First, a country nominates a candidate. Then the candidate shares a vision statement, a resume, and information about campaign money. Candidates also take part in public town halls and answer questions. Finally, the Security Council recommends someone, and the General Assembly appoints that person.

The next leader will face big challenges, including fixing the U.N.'s money problems, climate change, artificial intelligence, and tensions between countries. Experts say the job depends a lot on the person who gets it.
why_it_matters: The United Nations makes choices that touch kids everywhere, like how countries work together on climate and health, so who leads it can shape the world you grow up in.

background_read: The United Nations (a group where almost all countries meet to talk about big world problems) was started in 1945, after World War II ended.
Its top leader is called the secretary-general. The current one, António Guterres (the U.N. leader since 2017), is finishing his time in the job at the end of the year.
In all the years since 1945, a woman has never led the United Nations, so this race could make history.
Article_Structure: WHO: Seven candidates — four women and three men — from Ecuador, Argentina, Costa Rica, Uganda, Guyana and Senegal.
WHAT: They are competing to become the next secretary-general, the top official of the United Nations.
WHERE: The United Nations, whose members meet together and whose leaders come from countries all around the world.
WHY: The next leader must handle the U.N.'s money problems, climate change, artificial intelligence and tensions between countries.

perspectives.description: Some people are excited because, for the first time ever, the United Nations could be led by a woman.
Others say the process is too closed off, because in the end a few powerful countries on the Security Council really decide who gets the job.
Some experts say the person matters most of all — the job is so hard that the right leader could change more than any new rule.
